_note: Short paraphrased summaries written for this research demonstrator. They are NOT the guideline text and may be out of date. Replace with licensed, current guideline content and verify every statement before any clinical use.

cards.text: At the first assessment, categorise urinary incontinence in women as stress, urge (overactive bladder) or mixed, and start treatment on the basis of the main symptom. Overactive bladder means urgency, usually with frequency and nocturia, with or without urge incontinence.
cards.action: Record the predominant type of incontinence before choosing treatment.

cards.text: Use a bladder diary covering at least three days, including both usual work and leisure days, to record how often and how much urine is passed and episodes of urgency and leakage.
cards.action: Ask the patient to complete a bladder diary for at least three days.

cards.text: Carry out a urine dipstick test in women with urinary incontinence to look for blood, glucose, protein, leukocytes and nitrites. If there are symptoms of urinary infection and the dipstick is positive for leukocytes and nitrites, send urine for culture.
cards.action: Dipstick the urine and send culture if infection is suspected.

cards.text: Offer bladder training lasting at least six weeks as first-line treatment for women with urge or mixed urinary incontinence.
cards.action: Offer bladder training for at least six weeks as first-line treatment.

cards.text: Recommend a trial of reduced caffeine for women with overactive bladder, advise on modifying fluid intake that is unusually high or low, and advise weight loss where body mass index is over 30.
cards.action: Advise a trial of caffeine reduction and sensible fluid intake.

cards.text: Offer a trial of supervised pelvic floor muscle training of at least three months as first-line treatment for stress or mixed urinary incontinence.
cards.action: For mixed symptoms, add supervised pelvic floor training for at least three months.

cards.text: Before starting a medicine for overactive bladder, discuss the likely benefits, common side effects and the cumulative anticholinergic burden, particularly in older or frail women. Review a new overactive bladder medicine about four weeks after starting it.
cards.action: If medication is considered, assess anticholinergic burden and arrange a four-week review.

cards.text: Mirabegron is recommended as an option for overactive bladder symptoms only when antimuscarinic medicines are contraindicated, clinically ineffective or have unacceptable side effects.
cards.action: Consider mirabegron when antimuscarinics are unsuitable, checking blood pressure first.

cards.text: Mirabegron is contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension, and blood pressure should be measured before starting treatment and monitored regularly during it.
cards.action: Measure blood pressure before and during mirabegron treatment.

cards.section: Overactive bladder not responding to treatment
cards.text: When overactive bladder does not respond to conservative and drug treatment, refer for specialist review; invasive options such as bladder wall botulinum toxin A injection should be discussed by a multidisciplinary team, and patients must be willing and able to self-catheterise if needed.
cards.action: Refer refractory overactive bladder for specialist and multidisciplinary review.

cards.text: In women under 65, the key signs of lower urinary tract infection are burning or pain on passing urine, new night-time urination and cloudy urine. Two or more of these make infection likely; a urine dipstick can help where fewer are present.
cards.action: Check for burning, new nocturia and cloudy urine; consider a dipstick if fewer than two are present.

cards.text: Do not use urine dipsticks to diagnose urinary infection in adults aged 65 and over, because bacteria in the urine without infection is common; base the decision on symptoms and signs and send a culture.
cards.action: In people aged 65 and over, rely on symptoms and send urine for culture rather than using a dipstick.

cards.text: For non-pregnant women with lower urinary tract infection, consider self-care, a back-up antibiotic prescription or an immediate short antibiotic course, taking into account severity, risk of complications and previous culture results. Choose the antibiotic from current local and national guidance.
cards.action: Agree a self-care, back-up or immediate antibiotic plan using current prescribing guidance.

cards.text: For men and for pregnant women with lower urinary tract infection, send a urine sample for culture before starting antibiotics and offer an immediate antibiotic prescription, reviewing the choice when results are available.
cards.action: In men and pregnant women, send a culture before antibiotics.

cards.text: Advise people to seek help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not improve within 48 hours of starting antibiotics, or if they become systemically unwell, for example with fever or loin pain.
cards.action: Safety-net: return if worse, not improving in 48 hours, or feverish with loin pain.

cards.text: For recurrent urinary tract infection, send urine for culture with each suspected infection, review possible causes and refer men and some women for specialist assessment; consider whether repeated negative cultures point to another diagnosis.
cards.action: Send cultures with each episode and reconsider the diagnosis if cultures are repeatedly negative.

cards.text: Refer people aged 45 and over using a suspected cancer pathway if they have unexplained visible haematuria without urinary tract infection, or visible haematuria that persists or recurs after successful treatment of infection.
cards.action: Use the suspected cancer pathway for visible haematuria in people aged 45 and over.

cards.text: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome is an unpleasant sensation of pain, pressure or discomfort perceived to be related to the bladder, with lower urinary tract symptoms lasting more than six weeks, in the absence of infection or another identifiable cause.
cards.action: Confirm bladder-related pain with urinary symptoms for over six weeks and exclude infection and other causes.

cards.text: Basic assessment includes a careful history, physical examination and urinalysis, with urine culture where indicated, and a baseline record of symptoms and pain so that treatment response can be measured.
cards.action: Record baseline pain and symptom scores, examine, and test urine to exclude infection.

cards.text: Treatment is individualised and usually multimodal, starting with education, self-care and behaviour change such as avoiding personal dietary triggers, alongside pain management; treatments are not strictly tiered, and options are chosen by shared decision-making.
cards.action: Start with education, self-care, trigger avoidance and pain management, agreed with the patient.

cards.text: Cystoscopy should be considered to look for Hunner lesions when they are suspected or treatment is not working, because Hunner lesions can be treated directly with endoscopic therapy.
cards.action: Consider specialist cystoscopy to look for Hunner lesions if symptoms persist.

cards.text: Primary bladder pain syndrome is persistent or recurrent pain perceived in the bladder region with at least one other symptom, such as pain worsening with bladder filling or daytime or night-time frequency, with no proven infection or other obvious local disease.
cards.action: Look for pain that worsens as the bladder fills plus frequency, after excluding infection.

cards.text: Bladder pain syndrome is best managed with a multidisciplinary, person-centred approach that includes psychological support and pelvic floor physiotherapy where appropriate.
cards.action: Involve pain, physiotherapy and psychological support as part of a multidisciplinary plan.

cards.text: The ICIQ-OAB records daytime frequency, night-time urination, urgency and urge leakage, each scored 0 to 4, giving a total from 0 to 16 where higher scores mean more severe symptoms. The questionnaire is licensed and must be obtained from the ICIQ group.
cards.action: Use the licensed ICIQ-OAB questionnaire to record a baseline severity score.

cards.text: The O'Leary-Sant questionnaire has a symptom index scored 0 to 20 and a problem index scored 0 to 16, used to measure bladder pain syndrome severity and response to treatment.
cards.action: Record O'Leary-Sant symptom and problem index scores at baseline and follow-up.
